A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OCR-Reasoning benchmark, with matching authors, core dataset statistics, evaluation framework, and retained experiments. Their text, tables, figures, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original model accuracy, reasoning-process scores, CoT experiments, and qualitative error analyses in Tables 2–4 and Figures 5–6.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds model evaluations, scoring validation, few-shot experiments, error analysis, synthetic-data fine-tuning, and a prompt ablation.

M1.justification: The core benchmark construction and evaluation procedures remain. Appendix A.5 adds a limited methodological adaptation: replacing human annotators with DouBao-1.5-Vision-Pro to generate synthetic training data, then fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B. The proposed process-aware reward model is only future work.

E1.justification: The benchmark retains its reported 1,069 examples, six abilities, and 18 tasks. v2 adds direct model evaluation on conventional DocVQA, ChartQA, TextVQA, and OCRBench tasks in Table 6, plus synthetic training using DocVQA, InfoVQA, TextVQA, and ChartQA images. These extend dataset use within the existing text-rich domain; multilingual and multi-page expansion remains prospective.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Qwen2.5-32B with OCR, six additional multimodal models including GLM-4.1V-Thinking and DeepEyesV2, and a document-oriented group comprising mPLUG-DocOwl2, Docopilot, DocMark, and TokenVL. Table 4 expands its previously closed-source-only reasoning comparison to include 13 open-source and three document-oriented models.

E3.justification: The original zero-shot evaluation remains, but v2 introduces substantially different experimental designs: one- and three-shot prompting with additional demonstrations, synthetic-data fine-tuning, and a factorial comparison of official and generic CoT prompts. Section 3.3 also adds a 200-example answer-extraction check and human-versus-LLM scoring comparisons.

E4.justification: v2 adds scoring-pipeline validation, few-shot sensitivity analysis, a six-category DouBao error breakdown, a synthetic-training-data utility experiment, and an ablation testing the proposed VL-Rethinker prompt conflict. These address questions beyond v1's CoT comparison and illustrative cases. The earlier qualitative analyses are retained in Appendices A.2–A.4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The new human-versus-LLM score comparisons provide validation outcomes without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All original numerical entries in Tables 2–4 are retained, but substantial new results appear. The expanded model set raises the best reported open-source accuracy from Qwen2.5-VL-72B's 37.5% to GLM-4.1V-Thinking-9B's 44.1%. New Qwen2.5-VL-7B settings report 16.1% and 16.4% with few-shot prompting and 17.0% after fine-tuning, alongside the unchanged 15.7% zero-shot result. Additional reasoning scores, validation outcomes, benchmark comparisons, and diagnostic results are also reported.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs about the benchmark or models. The mathematical worked examples retain their reasoning, and v2's new scope and mechanism explanations do not introduce formal assumptions, derivations, or guarantees.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a benchmark with answer and reasoning annotations, and the claim that no evaluated MLLM exceeds 50% accuracy is retained. The introduction replaces v1's claim that open-source models remain below 40% with a claim that document-oriented models remain below 15%, consistent with the expanded comparisons.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation: it explains the single-image scope, attributes the error distribution primarily to higher-level reasoning, discusses guidance and input-length explanations for few-shot effects, and develops the official-prompt/CoT conflict hypothesis. Appendices A.5–A.6 extend the framework's stated applicability to training-data construction and outline future development. The original dataset-cost and LLM-judge limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the use of official RL-model prompts, additional few-shot demonstrations, and the generator, source datasets, and 5,000-image scale of synthetic training. However, v1's disclosure of eight A800 GPUs is removed, and fine-tuning hyperparameters remain unspecified. The existing repository link is retained; additional distribution channels are only planned.

R1.justification: The related-work structure and positioning around reasoning versus text extraction remain largely unchanged. v2 adds references supporting newer model comparisons and scope discussion, including Docopilot, DocMark, Marten, Keye-VL, Thyme, DeepEyesV2, GLM, and MiMo-VL. Publication updates and the author-year citation format do not constitute new research positioning.

P1.justification: v2 extensively edits the abstract, introduction, curation description, and conclusion, and reorganizes and consolidates the results narrative. Earlier qualitative discussion moves into separate appendix subsections, while the appendix gains a broader hierarchy. Author contribution notes, affiliations, acknowledgments, and citation style also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with a different illustrative chart, Figure 2 is comprehensively redesigned, and Figure 3 is restyled. Tables 2 and 4 expand, four new tables and an error-distribution figure appear, and earlier qualitative figures move to the appendix, including v1 Figure 5 becoming v2 Figure 8. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's empirical foundation. It extends reasoning-process evaluation beyond the five closed-source models, adds human checks of scoring, and tests a previously speculative prompt-conflict explanation through ablation. The error analysis further supports the benchmark's focus on reasoning difficulties. These gains outweigh the loss of GPU information, although human-validation procedures and fine-tuning settings remain insufficiently documented and uncertainty reporting is still absent.
